strategy_title: Hardcoded Tile Size Change Without Autotune Causes Regression
strategy_description: Changing BLOCK_M/BLOCK_N/BLOCK_K from 32/32/128 to 64/64/64 via hardcoded constexpr values (instead of using @triton.autotune) caused a 2.14x slowdown. The plan called for adding @triton.autotune but the implementation only changed the hardcoded constants, so the new tile sizes were never empirically validated. The larger tiles (64x64x64) increased register pressure from 94 to 128 registers/thread, reducing Block Limit Registers from 5 to 4 blocks/SM, and tripled the executed instruction count (3.1M → 9.9M) without improving occupancy (still 6.25%), resulting in 2.14x longer kernel duration (49.73 µs → 106.37 µs).
applicable_when: Kernel has severe shared memory bank conflicts (12-way, 77%+ conflict wavefront ratio) with BLOCK_K=128 and float32 elements; SharedMemoryConflicts NCU rule triggered with >70% speedup potential; occupancy limited by shared memory (Block Limit Shared Mem < Block Limit Registers).
do_not_apply_when: Do not change tile sizes via hardcoded constexpr without @triton.autotune — larger tiles increase register pressure and instruction count without guarantee of improvement. Never blindly increase BLOCK_M and BLOCK_N together with BLOCK_K reduction, as the combined effect on register file can negate any bank conflict savings. Avoid this pattern when registers_per_thread is already near 96 (the 128-register limit will reduce Block Limit Registers and worsen occupancy).
framework_notes: In Triton, tile sizes set as tl.constexpr inside the kernel body are fixed at compile time. To explore tile configurations, they must be promoted to kernel arguments decorated with @triton.autotune and the grid must be changed to a lambda (META dict). Simply changing the hardcoded values is an implementation flaw — the plan required autotune but the diff shows only constant reassignment. The grid was also not updated to match the new tile sizes (still 80 blocks hardcoded), which would have caused incorrect results with larger tiles anyway.
